> [!TLDR]
> Separate Kruskal patches extend the RN metric across its two horizons and reveal its repeated causal structure.

<!-- Source: PDF page 194, printed page 178. -->

The function $f(\mechanical{r})=1-2\mechanical{M}/\mechanical{r}+\electric{Q}^2/\mechanical{r}^2$ has zeros at $\mechanical{r}=\mechanical{r_\pm}$, where

$$
\mechanical{r_\pm}=\mechanical{M}\pm\sqrt{\mechanical{M}^2-\electric{Q}^2}. \tag{5.24}
$$

The roots are both real, and the RN spacetime truly contains a black hole, when $\lvert\electric{Q}\rvert\le\mechanical{M}$. The special case of a black hole with $\lvert\electric{Q}\rvert=\mechanical{M}$ is referred to as an *extreme* RN black hole. If $\lvert\electric{Q}\rvert>\mechanical{M}$, then the RN solution describes a *naked singularity* at $\mechanical{r}=0$.

The coordinates $(\mechanical{t},\mechanical{r})$ are singular at the outer horizon $(\mechanical{r}=\mechanical{r_+})$, and new coordinates must be introduced to extend the metric across this surface. This can be done with Kruskal coordinates. As we shall see, however, these coordinates fail to be regular at the inner horizon $(\mechanical{r}=\mechanical{r_-})$, and another coordinate transformation will be required to extend the metric beyond this surface. Thus, Kruskal coordinates are specific to a given horizon, and a single coordinate patch is not sufficient to cover the entire RN manifold (Fig. 5.8). We will see that the outer horizon in an event horizon for the RN spacetime, and the inner horizon is an apparent horizon.

Let us first take care of the extension across the outer horizon. We express the RN metric in the form

$$
\mathrm d\mechanical{s}^2=-f\,\mathrm d\mechanical{t}^2+f^{-1}\mathrm d\mechanical{r}^2+\mechanical{r}^2\mathrm d\Omega^2,
$$

where $f=1-2\mechanical{M}/\mechanical{r}+\electric{Q}^2/\mechanical{r}^2$. Near $\mechanical{r}=\mechanical{r_+}$ this function can be approximated by

$$
f(\mechanical{r})\simeq2\mechanical{\kappa_+}(\mechanical{r}-\mechanical{r_+}),
$$

where $\mechanical{\kappa_+}\equiv\frac12f'(\mechanical{r_+})$. It follows that near $\mechanical{r}=\mechanical{r_+}$,

$$
\mechanical{r^*}\equiv\int\frac{\mathrm d\mechanical{r}}{f}\simeq\frac{1}{2\mechanical{\kappa_+}}\ln\lvert\mechanical{\kappa_+}(\mechanical{r}-\mechanical{r_+})\rvert.
$$

**Fig. 5.8** Kruskal patches for the Reissner–Nordström spacetime.

<!-- Source: PDF page 195, printed page 179. -->

Introducing the null coordinates $\mechanical{u}=\mechanical{t}-\mechanical{r^*}$ and $\mechanical{v}=\mechanical{t}+\mechanical{r^*}$, the surface $\mechanical{r}=\mechanical{r_+}$ appears at $\mechanical{v}-\mechanical{u}=-\infty$ and we define the Kruskal coordinates $U_+$ and $V_+$ by

$$
U_+=\mp e^{-\mechanical{\kappa_+}\mechanical{u}},\qquad V_+=e^{\mechanical{\kappa_+}\mechanical{v}}. \tag{5.25}
$$

Here, the upper sign refers to $\mechanical{r}>\mechanical{r_+}$ and the lower sign refers to $\mechanical{r}<\mechanical{r_+}$. It is easy to check that $f\simeq-2U_+V_+$ near $\mechanical{r}=\mechanical{r_+}$, so that the metric becomes

$$
\mathrm d\mechanical{s}^2\simeq-\frac{2}{\mechanical{\kappa_+}^2}\,\mathrm dU_+\,\mathrm dV_++\mechanical{r_+}^2\mathrm d\Omega^2.
$$

This shows that when it is expressed in the coordinates $(U_+,V_+)$, the metric is well behaved at the outer horizon. On the other hand, an exact integration for $\mechanical{r^*}(\mechanical{r})$ would reveal that $\mechanical{r^*}\to+\infty$ at the inner horizon, which is then located at $\mechanical{v}-\mechanical{u}=\infty$, or $U_+V_+=\infty$. The Kruskal coordinates are singular at the inner horizon.

The coordinates $(U_+,V_+)$ should be used only in the interval $\mechanical{r_1}<\mechanical{r}<\infty$, where $\mechanical{r_1}>\mechanical{r_-}$ is some cutoff radius. Inside $\mechanical{r}=\mechanical{r_1}$ another coordinate system must be introduced. One such system is $(\mechanical{t},\mechanical{r})$, in which the metric takes the standard form of Eq. (5.21). It is important to understand that this new coordinate patch, which covers the portion of the RN spacetime corresponding to the interval $\mechanical{r_-}<\mechanical{r}<\mechanical{r_+}$, is *distinct* from the original patch that covers the external region $\mechanical{r}>\mechanical{r_+}$. And indeed, because $f$ is now negative, the new $\mechanical{t}$ must be interpreted as a spacelike coordinate (because $g_{tt}>0$) while $\mechanical{r}$ must be interpreted as a timelike coordinate (because $g_{rr}<0$).

There still remains the issue of extending the spacetime beyond $\mechanical{r}=\mechanical{r_-}$, where the new $(\mechanical{t},\mechanical{r})$ coordinates fail. We want to construct a new set of Kruskal coordinates, $U_-$ and $V_-$, adapted to the inner horizon. Retracing the same steps as before, we have that near $\mechanical{r}=\mechanical{r_-}$ the function $f$ can be approximated by

$$
f(\mechanical{r})\simeq-2\mechanical{\kappa_-}(\mechanical{r}-\mechanical{r_-}),
$$

where $\mechanical{\kappa_-}=\frac12\lvert f'(\mechanical{r_-})\rvert$. It follows that

$$
\mechanical{r^*}\simeq-\frac{1}{2\mechanical{\kappa_-}}\ln\lvert\mechanical{\kappa_-}(\mechanical{r}-\mechanical{r_-})\rvert.
$$

With $\mechanical{u}=\mechanical{t}-\mechanical{r^*}$ and $\mechanical{v}=\mechanical{t}+\mechanical{r^*}$, the surface $\mechanical{r}=\mechanical{r_-}$ appears at $\mechanical{v}-\mechanical{u}=+\infty$ and we define the new Kruskal coordinates by

$$
U_-=\mp e^{\mechanical{\kappa_-}\mechanical{u}},\qquad V_-=e^{-\mechanical{\kappa_-}\mechanical{v}}. \tag{5.26}
$$

Here, the upper sign refers to $\mechanical{r}>\mechanical{r_-}$ and the lower sign refers to $\mechanical{r}<\mechanical{r_-}$. Then $f\simeq-2U_-V_-$ and the metric becomes

$$
\mathrm d\mechanical{s}^2\simeq-\frac{2}{\mechanical{\kappa_-}^2}\,\mathrm dU_-\,\mathrm dV_-+\mechanical{r_-}^2\mathrm d\Omega^2.
$$

<!-- Source: PDF page 196, printed page 180. -->

This is manifestly regular across $\mechanical{r}=\mechanical{r_-}$. The new Kruskal coordinates, however, are singular at $\mechanical{r}=\mechanical{r_+}$.

What happens now on the other side of the inner horizon? The most noticeable feature is that the singularity at $\mechanical{r}=0$ appears as a *timelike* surface – this is markedly different from what happens inside a Schwarzschild black hole, where the singularity is spacelike. Because $f>0$ when $\mechanical{r}<\mechanical{r_-}$, $\mechanical{r}$ re-acquires its interpretation as a spacelike coordinate; any surface $\mechanical{r}=\text{constant}<\mechanical{r_-}$ is therefore a timelike hypersurface, and this includes the singularity. Because it is timelike, the singularity can be *avoided* by observers moving within the black hole. This is a striking new phenomenon, and we should examine it very carefully.

Consider the motion of a typical observer inside a RN black hole (Fig. 5.8). Before crossing the inner horizon (but after going across the outer horizon), $\mechanical{r}$ is a timelike coordinate and the motion necessarily proceeds with $\mechanical{r}$ decreasing. After crossing $\mechanical{r}=\mechanical{r_-}$, however, $\mechanical{r}$ becomes spacelike and both types of motion ($\mechanical{r}$ decreasing or increasing) become possible. Our observer may therefore decide to reverse course, and if she does, she will avoid $\mechanical{r}=0$ altogether. Her motion inside the inner horizon will then proceed with $\mechanical{r}$ increasing and she will cross, once more, the surface $\mechanical{r}=\mechanical{r_-}$. This, however, is *another* copy of the inner horizon, distinct from the one encountered previously. (Recall that there are two copies of each surface $\mechanical{r}=\text{constant}$ in a Kruskal diagram.) After entering this new $\mechanical{r}>\mechanical{r_-}$ region, our observer notices that $\mechanical{r}$ has once again become timelike, and she finds that reversing course is no longer possible: Her motion must proceed with $\mechanical{r}$ increasing and this brings her in the vicinity of another surface $\mechanical{r}=\mechanical{r_+}$. Because there is no reason for spacetime to just stop there, yet another Kruskal patch $(U_+,V_+)$ must be introduced to extend the RN metric beyond this horizon. The new Kruskal coordinates take over where the old patch $(U_-,V_-)$ leaves off, at the spacelike hypersurface $\mechanical{r}=\mechanical{r_1}$.

The ultimate conclusion to these considerations is that our observer eventually emerges out of the black hole, through another copy of the outer horizon, into a new asymptotically-flat universe. Her trip may not end there: Our observer could now decide to enter the RN black hole that resides in this new universe, and this entire cycle would repeat! It therefore appears that the RN metric describes more than just a single black hole. Indeed, it describes an infinite lattice of asymptotically-flat universes connected by black-hole tunnels.

Such a fantastic spacetime structure is best represented with a Penrose–Carter diagram (Fig. 5.9). The diagram shows that the region bounded by the surfaces $\mechanical{r}=\mechanical{r_+}$ and $\mechanical{r}=\mechanical{r_-}$ contains trapped surfaces: Both ingoing and outgoing light rays originating from this region converge toward the singularity. The outer and inner horizons are therefore apparent horizons, but only the outer horizon is an event horizon.

## Physical quantities

| Symbol | Unit | Quantity | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\mechanical{M}$ | $\unit{\mathrm m}$ | Black-hole mass | The mass in geometrized units. |
| $\electric{Q}$ | $\unit{\mathrm m}$ | Electric charge | The charge in geometrized electromagnetic units. |
| $\mechanical{r},\mechanical{r_\pm},\mechanical{r_1}$ | $\unit{\mathrm m}$ | Areal and horizon radii | The radius, horizon radii, and coordinate-patch cutoff. |
| $\mechanical{t},\mechanical{u},\mechanical{v},\mechanical{r^*}$ | $\unit{\mathrm m}$ | Time and radial coordinates | The static time, null coordinates, and tortoise coordinate. |
| $\mechanical{s}$ | $\unit{\mathrm m}$ | Spacetime interval | The interval in the RN metric. |
| $\mechanical{\kappa_\pm}$ | $\unit{\mathrm m^{-1}}$ | Horizon parameters | Half the magnitude of the radial derivative of f at each horizon. |
